title: Phase-space attention scheduler memo
body:
Purpose and scope:
This note captures a series of small, focused experiments exploring an adaptive kernel selection strategy for attention-heavy workloads. The goal is to map the phase-space (batch x seq_len x model_dim) where each kernel variant (FlashAttention, PagedAttention, fused-MHA, and single-op fused matmuls) gives the best p50/p99 latency and token throughput on our standard inference hardware.

Why we care:
- Our serving runtime currently picks kernels by simple heuristics (seq_len threshold + model type). We see 10–40% worse tail latency on mixed workloads where the seq_len distribution has a long tail.
- Choosing a slightly slower per-token kernel can reduce queues and drop p99 by >2x in some configurations. We need a compact representation of the operating regimes to drive a scheduler.

Hardware and baseline:
- Instance: rwi-gpu-a100-40gb (8GB reserved for system), CUDA 12.2, cuDNN 9.3, NCCL 2.19.
- Model: MPT-7B-inference-style and Llama-2-13B (FP16), KV cache enabled.
- Baseline kernels: flashattn v2 (fused QKV->attn->out path), paged-attn implementation (our on-disk PagedFlash branch), fused-MHA (custom fused matmul+attn primitive), and matmul + aten-attn fallback.
- Measurement: p50/p90/p99 latency over 10k samples per config, throughput measured as tokens/sec steady-state. Warmup 200 requests.

Experiment matrix (high-level):
- Batch sizes: 1, 2, 4, 8
- Sequence lengths: 8, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024
- Model dims: 2048 (MPT-7B-like), 4096 (Llama-13B-like)
- Kernel variants: flashattn, paged-attn, fused-MHA, fallback
- Workload shapes: uniform seq_len; mixed heavy-tail (80% short, 20% long); step (sudden bump to long seqs every 50 requests).

Representative command used (profiling harness):
- python tools/bench_attn.py --model llama-13b --kernel flashattn --batch 2 --seq-len 256 --warmup 200 --iters 10000 --profile nvprof --kv-cache true
- Collected metrics: wallclock latency per request, kernel-level cudaEvent timings, nsight traces for 1% of runs.

Key observations and raw numbers (summaries):
1) Small batch, short seq (batch=1, seq=8): flashattn wins on p50 (0.9ms) and p99 (1.6ms). paged-attn overhead of page management hurts. fused-MHA slightly worse on p50 but similar p99.
2) Batch=4, seq=128: fused-MHA is best for throughput (tokens/sec +22% vs flashattn) and p50 by ~15%, but p99 occasionally spikes due to kernel launch queuing when many small requests land concurrently.
3) Long sequences (seq>=512): paged-attn becomes competitive for memory-limited 40GB instances because it keeps working set smaller; p50 comparable to flashattn but p99 often better (by ~18%) for mixed workloads because memory fragmentation reduced retry/eviction events.
4) Mixed heavy-tail workload: an adaptive choice that routes long requests to paged-attn and short ones to flashattn reduces overall p99 by ~30% compared to always-flash baseline.
5) Step workload (sudden bursts of long seqs): static heuristics performed poorly — latency cliff observed as kernel scheduler hit a saturation point. An adaptive admission policy (delay/buffer long requests briefly to coalesce) plus switching long jobs to paged-attn mitigated the cliff.

Profiling anecdotes (why some tails happen):
- KV cache eviction/growing: when many long-seq requests are interleaved with short ones, the allocator churn causes paging and occasional CUDA OOM-retries in our layer that result in long retries and high p99. paged-attn's smaller resident set prevents this.
- Kernel launch/serialization: fused-MHA sometimes uses a different cuBLAS plan that causes longer launch times for specific dims (4096 with head=32). This shows as spikes in nsight trace where a kernel sits queued for 1–3ms.
- Tensor core underutilization: small seq & small batch combos waste tensor cores; FlashAttention's kernel has special-case code paths that maintain higher occupancy.

Heuristic rules derived (candidate scheduler rules):
- If seq_len <= 64 and batch <= 2: prefer flashattn.
- If seq_len between 64 and 256 and batch >= 4: prefer fused-MHA for throughput (unless observed queue depth > X).
- If seq_len >= 512 or resident_memory_fraction > 0.7: prefer paged-attn.
- If incoming request rate > sustained_threshold and long-tail fraction > 0.15: enable short buffering window (10–25ms) to coalesce and route to throughput-optimized kernel.
- Always monitor kernel queue depth and trigger fallback when p99 > SLO_margin.

Scheduler design notes (implementation sketch):
- Phase-space map: maintain an exponentially smoothed 3D histogram over (batch, seq_len, model_dim) with counts and per-kernel observed p99. Use this to predict which kernel likely minimizes p99 for new request shapes.
- Fast path: do a table lookup for most frequent (batch, seq_len bucket) combos.
- Adaptive fallback: if chosen kernel's queue depth > threshold or memory pressure high, re-evaluate and fall back to alternate kernel.
- Learning rate: decay old observations quickly for ephemeral experiments (window = 1h by default in prod).

Representative micro-logs (trimmed):
- [2024-11-20 11:03:12] batch=2 seq=256 kernel=flashattn p50=6.0ms p99=35ms tokens/sec=4200
- [2024-11-20 11:03:42] batch=2 seq=256 kernel=paged-attn p50=6.4ms p99=12ms tokens/sec=3680
- [2024-11-20 11:04:05] batch=4 seq=128 kernel=fused-MHA p50=3.1ms p99=9.4ms tokens/sec=5600
- [2024-11-20 11:04:32] batch=1 seq=1024 kernel=paged-attn p50=42ms p99=48ms tokens/sec=240

Failure modes observed during experiments:
- Heuristic thrash: rapid switch between kernels when a short burst of long requests appears, causing extra context cost. Need hysteresis.
- Measurement noise: per-request time sampling at high throughput misses short outliers; we must sample kernel timings asynchronously and use sketching for distribution estimates.
- Interference from other processes on the same GPU (infra testbeds): ensure isolation or measure under dedicated nodes.

Next actions and experiment backlog:
- A: Implement an in-memory phase-space table in runtime and run A/B in canary pool (A: static heuristics, B: phase-space lookup with fallback). Target: 2 weeks. Owner: Maya.
- B: Add lightweight kernel queue-depth exporter (per-kernel queue length, average launch wait) to runtime metrics. Owner: Ethan.
- C: Implement short buffering/coalescing window prototype (configurable 0–50ms) and test on step workload. Owner: Lina.
- D: Re-run long-seq paged-attn experiments on 80GB instance types to validate memory advantage scale. Owner: Ravi.

Open questions and discussion points:
- What is acceptable added latency for short coalescing windows in PLG-hosted API? Need product input on SLO trade-offs.
- Do we gate kernel switching by model version to avoid cross-version kernel plan variance?
- How to expose knobs to customers (e.g., prefer lowest p99 vs prefer max throughput)?

Appendix: quick checklist for reproducing a run
- Setup: CUDA/CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES env, Python virtualenv with our runtime wheel, pinned flashattn branch.
- Command: tools/bench_attn.py --model <m> --kernel <k> --batch <b> --seq-len <s> --kv-cache true --warmup 200 --iters 10000
- Profiling: use nvprof for per-kernel times; save nsight traces for sample runs; collect dmesg and nvidia-smi during runs.

If helpful I can convert this into a small RFC with graphs and a proposed scheduler protobuf and start a PR for the phase-space table.

-- Ravi
